additions.title: R (Bridges) v Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058
additions.publisher: Court of Appeal (Civil Division); The National Archives, Find Case Law
additions.locator: Paragraphs 152-154 (data protection impact assessment); paragraphs 199-201 (public sector equality duty)
additions.quote: the DPIA failed properly to assess the risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
additions.why: The leading UK judgment on both halves of the question. The force had written an impact assessment for live facial recognition, and the court still held it inadequate because it did not grapple with the rights engaged; it also held that the force had 'not done all that they reasonably could' to meet the equality duty, never having checked the software for race or sex bias. Decided under section 64 of the Data Protection Act 2018 (law enforcement processing), not Article 35, and concerns a police force.

additions.title: Chelmer Valley High School (reprimand)
additions.quote: The school failed to complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) prior to introducing facial recognition technology for the purposes of cashless catering.
additions.why: Regulator enforcement on timing: a reprimand under Article 35(1) for putting a biometric system into use with no prior assessment. A reprimand, not a fine, against a school; only the regulator's summary page was read, not the reprimand document.

additions.title: Data protection impact assessments: When do we need to do a DPIA?
additions.locator: Section 'What does the ICO consider likely to result in high risk?', item 'Innovative technology'; section 'What does 'innovative technologies' mean?'
additions.quote: processing involving the use of innovative technologies, or the novel application of existing technologies (including AI)
additions.why: The screening rule behind the middle level of the question: the regulator's Art. 35(4) list names AI as innovative technology, and an assessment is required when that is combined with another listed factor such as evaluation or scoring. Marked under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. No date printed on the page; the year given is the year it was read.

additions.title: Ethics, Transparency and Accountability Framework for Automated Decision-Making
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology; Centre for Data Ethics and Innovation; Cabinet Office; Office for Artificial Intelligence
additions.locator: Point 2 'Deliver fair services for all of our users and citizens', practical steps; point 1 'Test to avoid any unintended outcomes or consequences'
additions.quote: You must do an Equality Impact Assessment to adhere to the Equality Act (2010) and Public Sector Equality Duty
additions.why: Government's own instruction to departments to run the equality and data protection assessments together and regularly. It goes further than the statute, which requires due regard and does not name an assessment document. Guidance for government departments only; last updated 2023.

additions.title: Introduction to AI assurance
additions.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
additions.locator: Section 4 'The AI assurance toolkit', list of assurance mechanisms
additions.quote: Used to anticipate the wider effects of a system/product on the environment, equality, human rights, data protection, or other outcomes.
additions.why: Places the impact assessment among assurance mechanisms, alongside audit and conformity assessment by third parties, which bears on the top level of the question (assessments independently assured). Introductory guidance with no legal force.

additions.title: A systematic review of artificial intelligence impact assessments
additions.publisher: Artificial Intelligence Review (Springer Nature); B. C. Stahl and others
additions.quote: Working with a population of 181 documents, the authors identified 38 actual AI-IAs and subjected them to a rigorous qualitative analysis
additions.why: Peer-reviewed systematic review, open access, led from a UK university. Finds some convergence in what AI impact assessments cover but warns of fragmentation and of grading that is open to interpretation, which is the case for one joined template. Literature search ran January to June 2021, so it pre-dates the AI Act's fundamental rights assessment.

additions.title: An Institutional View of Algorithmic Impact Assessments
additions.publisher: Harvard Journal of Law & Technology, Volume 35, Number 1; A. D. Selbst
additions.locator: Abstract; body text on documentation and discrimination law (passage before footnote 100)
additions.quote: The ex ante documentation requirement enables the possibility of an ex post remedy.
additions.why: Explains why an assessment done before deployment matters to the people affected: it creates the record that later lets a harm be proved and put right. Also argues that a regime relying on firms' own discretion can be undermined by their incentives. United States law review article, edited by students and not peer reviewed in the journal sense; written about US law.

additions.title: Algorithmic impact assessment: a case study in healthcare
additions.quote: AIAs are currently largely untested in public-sector contexts.
additions.why: UK evidence: a worked proposal for an impact assessment, with public participation and publication, as a condition of access to NHS imaging data. Useful for the levels that ask about consultation and publishing. A proposal for one programme, published by a research institute and not peer reviewed; dated 2022.

additions.title: NSW AI Assessment Framework
additions.locator: Sections 'What is it?' and 'When should it be used?'
additions.quote: reassessed when there are significant changes to their features, datasets, purpose or decision-making contexts
additions.why: International comparator: a mandatory assessment covering fairness, privacy, transparency and accountability together, started early and repeated on change, for AI that is bought as well as built. New South Wales public sector only, under Circular DCS-2026-02; a self-assessment, with independent review only for high and critical risk. No date printed on the page.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. Bridges (Court of Appeal, 2020) supports it and could be named: an impact assessment existed and was still held inadequate, and the equality duty was breached. Note that Cabinet Office guidance tells departments they 'must do an Equality Impact Assessment', which is stronger than the statute; the brief's wording (due regard) is the accurate one.
